🤖 THREEHALVES — THE CENTAUR ROBOT Threehalves is a 7-foot-tall teleoperated robot developed by Satyress. Its design combines a human-like torso and arms with a powerful four-legged chassis, creating a mechanical centaur built for environments that are too dangerous for humans. The idea behind Threehalves is simple: instead of sending a person into extreme heat, unstable terrain, darkness, hazardous industrial environments or disaster zones, a skilled operator can control the robot remotely and perform the work from a safer location. Unlike many humanoid robots, Threehalves is designed around tools and equipment that humans already use. Its modular limbs and quick-connect system allow it to be adapted for different tasks, while its four-legged platform provides stability on difficult terrain. The most unsettling part is probably its appearance. With its enormous size, humanoid body, four mechanical legs and distinctive horned head, Threehalves looks less like a traditional industrial machine and more like something from a science-fiction horror movie. But behind the terrifying design is a serious engineering concept: putting the machine in danger instead of the human. Threehalves is still a developing robotics project, but it represents a strange glimpse into a future where dangerous jobs could be performed remotely — with a human controlling the machine from a distance. And honestly… it might be one of the creepiest robots ever built. 👁️ #threehalves #robot #baal #satyress #horrortok

Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, organisers said. In a 100-metre sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88m, well above the 0.95m best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45m set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. The five-day games, now in their second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the US heats up. There are 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place, including running, table tennis and football. For more news, visit @sbsnews_au (link in bio).

videos.caption: Hugging Face and its Pollen Robotics subsidiary have opened preorders for Microduck, a $399 desktop-sized robot built for experimenting with “physical AI.”  The 25cm robot contains 15 motors, a camera, a depth sensor, two inertial measurement units, and a “beak” that can grasp small objects.  Its open-source software allows developers to train behaviors through reinforcement learning in a physics simulator before transferring them to the real machine.  Microduck can already walk, crouch, follow a laser, grab objects, and recover from many falls.  More than 10,000 units were preordered in its first five days, roughly $4 million! Initial deliveries are targeted before Christmas of this year in North America, Europe, and the UK. Would you buy one?

Researchers at the Italian Institute of Technology (IIT) have successfully demonstrated iRonCub, a jet-powered humanoid robot capable of hovering mid-air. Instead of walking or running, the robot achieves flight and maintains perfect balance by utilizing four jet thrusters—two mounted on its arms and two on a back jetpack. Built with a titanium spine and heat-resistant covers to endure the extreme forces of flight, iRonCub is being developed to eventually assist in search-and-rescue missions and conduct inspections in hazardous, hard-to-reach environments. space Science robot humanoid

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

MicroDuck is the kind of small humanoid robot that makes you want to look closer at the engineering. Small bipedal robots are useful for exploring ideas in locomotion, balance, joint control and robot learning without needing a full-sized humanoid platform. What interests me most is the combination of accessible hardware and motion learning. When robot designs and control methods are available to the community, researchers and developers can study how the robot moves, reproduce experiments and build on existing work. For bipedal robots, getting the model to walk is only one part of the job. The robot also needs to manage its balance, respond to changes in contact with the ground and recover when its motion deviates from the target. That is where simulation, reinforcement learning and real-world testing become relevant. A motion policy that works in simulation still needs to prove itself on physical hardware, where friction, motor limits and imperfect contact can affect the result. MicroDuck is worth following from this perspective. Small platforms can make robotics experiments more accessible, especially when the community can inspect the design and the software behind the movement. I’m interested in seeing how far this approach can go, from basic walking to more reliable dynamic motions. How much progress in humanoid locomotion could come from more open, low-cost platforms that people can actually build and test? #Robotics #HumanoidRobots #OpenSource #PhysicalAI

What if a humanoid robot could clean your home while you focus on other things? Meet Tau Robotics, a startup bringing humanoid robots into real homes to perform everyday cleaning tasks. The robots can vacuum floors, mop, wipe surfaces and clean toilets. They are designed to handle the kind of repetitive work that many people would rather avoid. But there is an important technical detail. These robots are not fully autonomous yet. A human operator controls them remotely through onboard cameras, while AI assists with the work. Each cleaning session also generates real-world data that Tau Robotics uses to train its AI models for future autonomous tasks. This approach gives the team a way to test humanoid robotics in unpredictable environments such as kitchens, living rooms and hallways. Real homes present challenges that are difficult to reproduce in a laboratory, from objects in unexpected places to tasks requiring precise hand movements. The current limitations are worth watching too. Fine manipulation, folding laundry and loading dishwashers remain difficult for humanoid robots. I find the use of real homes as training environments interesting. Every cleaning session can reveal where the robot struggles and what its AI needs to learn next. The long-term goal is to move from remote human control toward greater autonomy. Would you let a remotely operated humanoid robot clean your home? #TauRobotics #HumanoidRobots #Robotics #PhysicalAI #EmbodiedAI

This piece is going to become a robot, although right now it is still at the stage where the structure does most of the talking. The armature is made from thick wire, fixed onto a wooden base, and the surface is starting to take shape with epoxy putty and found objects, including fragments of toys and other small elements. It is a process of building from whatever works best, combining sculptural modelling with materials that already carry their own strange character. One of the most useful tricks in this kind of work is surprisingly simple: cut plastic spoons. For @tomasbarcelocastela, they are a practical way to create large, smooth, geometric forms very quickly. They can be trimmed into different shapes and used as a base to establish these clean volumes before continuing to model over the top.
